articles.body:
A small power plant in the UK was shut down for four days in July following a cyberattack carried out by hackers linked to Iran, The Telegraph reported on Sunday. The incident happened around the time US authorities including the FBI warned about malicious cyber actors targeting water facilities across at least seven states — a warning in which CISA, the FBI, the EPA and other agencies blamed Iran.

**The UK response is careful in a specific way.** A government spokesperson declined to attribute blame or identify the facility. "This story refers to an incident impacting a small-scale energy generator, and at no point was there a risk to the wider energy system," the spokesperson told CNBC. "The U.K. has a highly resilient energy system. We work closely with the energy sector to protect infrastructure and ensure the highest security standards." The Department of Energy Security and Net Zero said it briefed energy CEOs, wrote to companies advising next steps, and is updating its cybersecurity regulations.

Read those two facts together: no attribution, no naming, insistence on containment — and simultaneously a CEO-level briefing round and a regulatory revision. Governments do not rewrite cybersecurity regulations over an incident they consider unimportant. Non-attribution is a policy choice, not an absence of knowledge, because naming a state actor as having taken down civilian power creates an obligation to respond.

**The pattern this fits.** Cyber experts warned of Iranian attacks on Western businesses and infrastructure shortly after the US and Israel launched their war on Iran on 28 February. On 18 August the US Department of Justice charged 17 Iranians with conducting a "massive cyber theft campaign on behalf of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and other Iranian entities". This is the asymmetric register of the conflict: a state under naval blockade and facing what Washington calls the greatest financial offensive ever mounted has limited conventional options and considerable cyber capability, and civilian infrastructure in countries supporting the sanctions regime is the accessible target.

**It runs both ways.** In June, blockchain analytics firm Elliptic reported that Iran's largest cryptocurrency exchange, Nobitex, was hacked for more than $90 million. The funds were drained into addresses bearing anti-government messages explicitly referencing the IRGC — pointing to a politically motivated attack rather than theft.

**Why a "small-scale generator" is the interesting detail.** Large utilities have security budgets, regulatory obligations and dedicated operational-technology teams. Small independent generators, water treatment plants and distribution operators often do not, while being connected to the same grid and running the same industrial control systems. The FBI's water-facility warning describes exactly this class of target. An attacker probing for the weakest link in a national system will find it at the edge, and four days of downtime at the edge is a proof of concept, not the objective.

**What it means for an Indian investor and operator.** India's power, water, port and airport operators run comparable control systems, and India's position on Iran — continued energy relationships, non-participation in the sanctions regime — is different from the UK's, which cuts both ways on targeting risk. The direct commercial read is that OT security is becoming a mandated spend rather than a discretionary one: the UK is updating its regulations, and that pattern travels. Indian IT services and cybersecurity firms selling into utilities, and the domestic startups building industrial security tools, are on the receiving end of that budget. Note the same week's reporting that Indian cybersecurity startups are looking overseas for growth, and that a consortium including banks and regulators has launched a cross-regional post-quantum security pilot.

**Confidence note.** Single-sourced to The Telegraph, with the UK government explicitly declining to attribute the attack or name the facility. The DoJ indictment and the FBI water-facility warning are independently on the record; the specific UK power plant attribution is not.

**What to watch.** Whether the UK names the actor; the content of the revised cybersecurity regulations; further incidents at small generators or water utilities; and CERT-In advisories in India.

articles.body:
Third Wave Coffee has raised ₹408 crore ($43 million) led by existing investor WestBridge Capital, with most of the capital coming through a primary issuance and participation from existing investor Creaegis and angel investors. Per a Mint report, the round values the Bengaluru chain at around ₹2,000 crore ($210 million), up from ₹1,200 crore ($150 million) in its previous round.

**The primary-issuance detail matters.** "Most of the capital coming through a primary issuance" means the money is going into the business rather than to selling shareholders. In a market where several recent rounds have been insider-funded or secondary-heavy, a large primary round with a 67% valuation step-up is a genuine vote of confidence from an investor who has been on the cap table since Series A.

**The plan.** Expansion in existing markets, presence in high-potential cities, and acceleration of the Third Rush Desserts segment. Nine new cities are planned in coming months including Ludhiana, Jalandhar, Amritsar and Lucknow, with deeper penetration of tier II and tier III towns. The company, founded in 2017 by Sushant Goel, Ayush Bathwal and Anirudh Sharma, currently operates across Bengaluru, Delhi, Pune, Mumbai and Hyderabad, and also sells coffee beans and cold brew bags. WestBridge led the $21 million Series B in 2022; Creaegis led a $35 million Series C in 2023. Total funding now exceeds $105 million.

**The history is not uncomplicated, and that is useful context.** Soon after the 2023 raise, Third Wave laid off around 100 employees. Around the same time co-founder and then-CEO Sushant Goel stepped down to the board, and Rajat Luthra, former CEO of KFC India and Nepal, was brought in to replace him. In FY25 operating revenue stood at ₹285 crore with a net loss of ₹94 crore — a loss that was narrowing. FY26 financials have not been filed. So the picture is a company that over-expanded, brought in an operator from quick-service restaurants, cut costs, improved its loss trajectory, and has now raised a large primary round to expand again — this time into smaller cities where rents and competitive intensity are lower and Starbucks and Blue Tokai are thinner on the ground.

**The second round of the day.** D2C skincare brand Asaya raised ₹88 crore ($9.2 million) from RPSG Capital, OTP Ventures, Huddle Ventures, Hyperscale Ventures and 72 Ventures at a ₹400 crore post-money valuation, comprising primary and secondary capital with some early angels selling out. It had raised ₹28 crore in a pre-Series A last September. Founded in 2021 by Neeraj Biyani, Eeti Sharma and Mandeep Singh Bhatia, Asaya targets hyperpigmentation, dehydration and acne, and has developed a proprietary molecule it calls MelaMe aimed at pigmentation in Indian skin types. Proceeds go to R&D, product expansion, distribution and hiring. It sells through its own channels, quick commerce and select offline retail.

**The sector pattern.** Indian D2C skincare has drawn steady investor interest around science-backed, ingredient-led positioning: RAS Luxury Skincare took ₹60 crore from Dabur in March 2026, Chosen raised $5 million led by Fireside in May, KorinMi ₹10 crore from Lotus Herbals' innovation fund in June, and Clarity Labs over ₹4 crore in seed. Strategic money from established FMCG houses is increasingly the exit route.

**What it means for an Indian investor.** Both rounds point the same way: capital is available for consumer brands that can show either unit-level discipline (Third Wave's narrowing loss and operator-led turnaround) or genuine product differentiation (Asaya's proprietary molecule). Neither is a growth-at-any-cost round. For public-market investors, Third Wave's ₹2,000 crore valuation on ₹285 crore of FY25 revenue is a roughly 7x sales mark for an unprofitable café chain — a useful private comparable when assessing listed QSR and café multiples, and a reminder that the private market is still paying up for physical-retail consumer scale.

**What to watch.** Third Wave's FY26 filings for whether the loss kept narrowing; store count and same-store sales in the new tier II/III cities; and whether an FMCG strategic bids for Asaya.

articles.body:
Iran's National Security Commission approved Article 3 of the "Strategic Action to Ensure the Security and Progress of the Strait of Hormuz" plan on Sunday. Under it, ships from countries authorised to pass through the strait will pay Iran for services it provides. Commission spokesperson Ebrahim Rezaei told state broadcaster IRIB the fees cover "navigation, environmental, fueling under certain conditions, insurance, safety and other services we provide", and that they "will be charged in Rials or any other currency desired by the Islamic Republic of Iran".

By Monday the enforcement architecture had arrived. Iran's Ports and Maritime Organization (PGSA) posted that "vessels violating Iranian protocols for the Strait of Hormuz shall face restrictions on future passages, including fines, detention, or confiscation" — and that "effective immediately, any vessel cooperating with listed vessels (via STS, transshipment, etc.) will be added to the list." Cargo owners shipping to or from the Persian Gulf were told to check the Non-Compliant Vessels list before chartering; delisting requires a formal application with justifications to a PGSA email address.

**What has actually been built here.** Not a blockade in the conventional sense. A permissioning regime: a list of authorised countries, a list of non-compliant vessels, a fee schedule, an appeals process, and a contagion rule that penalises anyone who trades with the penalised. It is administrative rather than kinetic, and it is designed to be survivable — Iran collects revenue and asserts jurisdiction over a waterway through which roughly a fifth of the world's seaborne oil moved before the war, while giving compliant traffic a legal-looking way to keep moving.

**The legal manoeuvre.** Under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, a coastal state may not levy charges on ships merely for transit through a strait used for international navigation, but it may recover the cost of specific services actually rendered. Calling a toll a "service fee" for navigation, environmental and safety provision is the workaround. Payment "in rials or any other currency desired by the Islamic Republic" is the second manoeuvre — a mechanism to route hard currency into a sanctioned banking system, or to force rial demand, at exactly the moment Washington is trying to sever Iran's financial arteries.

**Both sides claim the water.** Supreme National Security Council secretary Mohsen Rezaei said on Saturday that "the Strait of Hormuz is closed, despite American claims, and will not open until America corrects its behaviour," adding "this time, America must first fulfil its obligations." He argued Washington has abandoned military options for economic pressure, and claimed Netanyahu assured Trump an economic blockade would force Iran to surrender. Trump, meanwhile, posted an image on Truth Social depicting the strait as "NEW US Territory". Rezaei also warned that "any country that becomes a partner in creating economic restrictions against us will be regarded by us as an enemy".

**The traffic data is the reality check.** Kpler counted four transits on Sunday, 13 on Saturday, 16 on Friday — fewer than 20 for the weekend, and possibly undercounted because ships are going dark. UKMTO logged 89 exits and 103 entries in the week to 21 August, with AIS-detected transits roughly 90% below pre-conflict baselines and declining since the 24-26 June peak. Tankers were 45% of traffic; of those, 56% carried crude, products or chemicals and 24% were LPG carriers. Two empty VLCCs entered dark on Friday. UKMTO has recorded 23 projectile-strike incidents since 6 July. A toll booth on a road carrying a tenth of its normal traffic collects very little.

**What it means for an Indian investor.** India is among the largest users of this corridor for crude, LPG and fertiliser feedstock. A formal fee regime plus a non-compliant-vessel list raises the landed cost of Gulf cargo through three channels — the fee itself, war-risk insurance premiums, and the compliance burden of screening charters against an Iranian list while also screening against US sanctions lists. Those two lists can conflict, which is a genuine operational problem for Indian refiners, shipowners and their insurers. It is also why India's diversification toward Venezuelan, Russian and West African barrels is accelerating. Watch LPG specifically: 24% of Hormuz traffic, and India's domestic cooking-gas subsidy is exposed to it.

**What to watch.** Whether any major shipowner actually pays; the composition of the authorised-countries list; daily transit counts; and Gulf war-risk insurance quotes.
